questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the key difference between a compiled language and an interpreted language?
options: Compiled languages run faster on every single processor, with no exceptions

A compiled language translates the entire program into executable form before anything runs and checks for structural correctness up front; an interpreted language translates and runs code line by line as it goes
Interpreted languages cannot have variables
There is no real difference between the two categories
questions.explain: The lesson defines compiled languages as translating and structurally checking the whole program before execution, while interpreted languages translate and run line by line with no separate upfront pass.

questions.q: Why does Apex give compile-time errors and runtime errors as two distinct categories?
options: Because Apex is a compiled language -- the platform compiles and structurally checks the code before it runs (catching compile-time errors), while other mistakes only surface once execution actually reaches the broken line (runtime errors)
Because Apex has no concept of errors at all
Because runtime errors are always more severe than compile-time errors
Because Apex only checks for errors if System.debug is called
questions.explain: Apex compiles code and checks its structure before execution begins, which is why structural mistakes are caught as compile-time errors, while other mistakes (like dividing by zero) only appear once execution actually reaches that line.

questions.q: In the two-line example `Integer total = 10 + 5; System.debug(total);`, what would happen if the two lines were swapped?
options: Nothing would change -- order doesn't matter in Apex
The program would run twice as fast
The second line would fail, because `total` would not yet exist when `System.debug` tried to use it
Apex would automatically reorder the lines correctly
questions.explain: The lesson's point is that instructions execute strictly in order -- `total` is only created and assigned on the first line, so referencing it before that line runs would fail.

questions.q: What is 'sequential execution,' as this lesson defines it?
options: A program's default behavior of running instructions one after another, top to bottom, unless something like control flow or a function call changes which instruction runs next
A technique used only in compiled languages
A way of running multiple instructions at the exact same instant
A synonym for a compile-time error
questions.explain: Sequential execution is the lesson's term for a program's default top-to-bottom order; control flow and functions are the two mechanisms that change which instruction runs next, without breaking the underlying in-order execution.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why can a program run successfully for a while and then fail partway through?
options: This can never happen -- a program either fails immediately or never fails
Because compile-time errors only appear after a random delay
Because a runtime error only occurs once execution actually reaches the specific broken instruction, which may be several lines into otherwise-working code
Because Apex programs restart themselves every few seconds
questions.explain: Runtime errors, unlike compile-time errors, only surface once execution reaches the specific line that's broken -- so a program can execute correctly for a while and then fail when it gets there.
